CHAPTER 2.1 · LEARNING AREA 2

CHAPTER 2.1 · LEARNING AREA 2 · NOVEMBER · DECEMBER

Assignments

Every pupil has a first name, every time of day a temperature, every throw a score. Assignments like these are everywhere in everyday life. You learn to represent them with arrows, tables, charts and equations, and you keep count of how often something happens in chance experiments.

12 LESSONS3 UNITS2 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • recognise assignments from everyday life and represent them with arrows
  • distinguish many-valued, single-valued and one-to-one assignments
  • represent an assignment in words, as a table, in a chart and as an equation
  • find and compare absolute and relative frequencies
CHECK-IN: CAN YOU ALREADY DO THIS?

How many minutes are $1.5$ hours?

$1.5 \cdot 60 = 90$

3 exercise books cost €6. What does one exercise book cost?

$6 : 3 = 2$

One box in a bar chart stands for 5 people. How many people does a bar 4 boxes high show?

$4 \cdot 5 = 20$

What percentage is 3 out of 4?

$\tfrac34 = 75\%$

WHO BELONGS TO WHOM?

Write the names of your group on the left of a sheet and the twelve months on the right. Draw arrows from each name to the month of birth.

  • Can more than one arrow start from a name? Can a month get more than one arrow?
  • What changes if the arrows point the other way?

  • Enter the values in a table and draw a chart.

📌 Throw a drawing pin 50 times. It lands on its back (point up) or on its side.

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Assignments around us

Exactly one arrow goes from each name to a month, because everyone has exactly one month of birth. The other way round it is different: several names can belong to one month, and none at all to another.

In an assignment the elements of a first set are assigned elements of a second set. In an arrow diagram an arrow points from each element to what is assigned to it. Depending on how many arrows start and arrive, there are three kinds.

KEY POINT · KINDS OF ASSIGNMENT

many-valued: several arrows start from at least one element.   number → its factors

single-valued: exactly one arrow starts from each element.   pupil → month of birth

one-to-one: single-valued, and single-valued backwards too: exactly one arrow arrives at each element of the second set.   pupil → seat

Reading backwards: if you turn all the arrows round, you get a new assignment. “Pupil → first name” becomes “first name → pupil”.

In geometry: if you reflect a figure, each point has exactly one image point and vice versa. That is one-to-one.

INTERACTIVE · WHICH KIND IS IT?

Choose an assignment, count the arrows and decide. The reason appears below.

EXAMPLE 1 · MULTIPLES

Each number is assigned its multiples: $3 \mapsto 3, 6, 9, 12, \ldots$ What kind of assignment is that?

Infinitely many arrows start from 3.

many-valued. If, on the other hand, each number is assigned only its triple, it is single-valued: $3 \mapsto 9$.

EXAMPLE 2 · MONTH AND DAYS

Each month of a year (not a leap year) is assigned its number of days. What kind is that?

Each month has exactly one number of days: single-valued. But seven arrows arrive at 31.

single-valued, but not one-to-one

EXERCISES

Draw an arrow diagram and decide which kind it is: a) the numbers $\{2, 3, 4, 5\}$ → their double   b) the numbers $\{4, 6, 9\}$ → their factors greater than 1

a) $2 \mapsto 4$, $3 \mapsto 6$, $4 \mapsto 8$, $5 \mapsto 10$: one-to-one   b) $4 \mapsto 2, 4$; $6 \mapsto 2, 3, 6$; $9 \mapsto 3, 9$: many-valued

What kind of assignment is it? a) car → number plate   b) person → birthday   c) book → number of pages   d) school class → its pupils

a) one-to-one (each number plate exists only once)   b) single-valued, not one-to-one   c) single-valued, not one-to-one   d) many-valued, because many pupils belong to one class

Think of an example from everyday life for each: a many-valued, a single-valued and a one-to-one assignment.

For example: football club → its players (many-valued), player → colour of shirt (single-valued), players of a team → shirt number (one-to-one).

Each natural number from 1 to 10 is assigned its remainder when divided by 4. Draw the arrows. How many arrows arrive at each remainder?

Remainder 0: 4, 8. Remainder 1: 1, 5, 9. Remainder 2: 2, 6, 10. Remainder 3: 3, 7. So 2, 3, 3 and 2 arrows. The assignment is single-valued, but not one-to-one.

A single-valued assignment goes from a set with 5 elements to a set with 3 elements. Can it be one-to-one? Justify.

How many arrows start altogether? How many may arrive on the right at most?

No. 5 arrows start, and there are only 3 targets on the right. So at least one target gets two arrows.

TEST YOURSELF!

Each number is assigned its factors. How many arrows start from 12?

$1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12$: six arrows.

Each month is assigned its number of days. How many arrows arrive at 31?

January, March, May, July, August, October, December: seven.

In a one-to-one assignment, how many arrows arrive at each element of the second set?

Exactly one.

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Representing assignments

A candle is 20 cm high and burns down 2.5 cm every hour. After 1 hour it is 17.5 cm high, after 2 hours 15 cm, and after 8 hours it is out. That is an assignment: time → height. You can write it down in four ways.

The description in words describes the assignment in sentences. The table (table of values) lists values that belong together. In the chart each pair becomes a point in the coordinate system: the first quantity to the right, the second upwards. Sometimes there is also an equation with which you can work out every value.

KEY POINT · FOUR REPRESENTATIONS

In words: “Every hour the candle burns down 2.5 cm.”

Table: time $t$ in h: $0, 1, 2, \ldots$   height $h$ in cm: $20; 17.5; 15; \ldots$

Chart: label the axes with the quantity and the unit. Only join the points if the values in between make sense too.

Equation: $h = 20 - 2.5 \cdot t$

Axes: the scale must be even. One box always stands for the same amount.

There is not always an equation. The temperature during a day or the weight of a baby can only be measured.

INTERACTIVE · ONE ASSIGNMENT, FOUR REPRESENTATIONS

Choose a row of the table. The same value lights up in the chart.

EXAMPLE 3 · READING FROM THE CHART

Choose “Temperature” above. How warm was it at 12 o’clock? When was it warmest? When was it 10 °C?

At 12 o’clock it was 14 °C. It was warmest at 14:00 with 15 °C.

10 °C at 10:00, and once more in the evening between 16:00 and 18:00.

EXAMPLE 4 · WITH THE EQUATION

How high is the candle after 6 hours? After how many hours is it only 7.5 cm high?

$h = 20 - 2.5 \cdot 6 = 20 - 15 = 5$ cm. For 7.5 cm, $12.5$ cm must burn down: $12.5 : 2.5 = 5$.

5 cm after 6 hours; 7.5 cm after 5 hours

EXERCISES

A swimming pool costs €3 entry per person. Make a table for 1 to 6 people and draw a chart. May you join the points?

1 → €3, 2 → €6, 3 → €9, 4 → €12, 5 → €15, 6 → €18. No: there are no half people, so only separate points.

A water tank holds 300 ℓ. 25 ℓ flow out per minute. Write an equation for the amount of water $w$ after $t$ minutes. When is the tank empty?

$w = 300 - 25 \cdot t$. Empty after $300 : 25 = 12$ minutes.

Describe in words: a) $p = 0.5 \cdot n$ ($n$ scoops of ice cream, price $p$ in €)   b) $k = 4 + 1.5 \cdot s$ ($s$ hours, cost $k$ in €)

a) One scoop costs €0.50.   b) There is a basic fee of €4 plus €1.50 for every hour.

Tim’s height: at 6 years 118 cm, at 8 years 128 cm, at 10 years 139 cm, at 12 years 152 cm. Draw a chart. Estimate how tall he was at 9. Can you predict his height at 30 from the chart?

At 9 years about 133 cm. At 30 years no: people stop growing at some point, so the points do not simply carry on like this.

Two candles are lit at the same time. Candle A is 20 cm high and burns down 2.5 cm per hour; candle B is 15 cm high and burns down 1.5 cm per hour. When are they the same height?

Make a table: every hour B catches up by 1 cm.

At the start A is 5 cm taller. Every hour the difference gets 1 cm smaller. After 5 hours both are $7.5$ cm high.

TEST YOURSELF!

$h = 20 - 2.5 \cdot t$. How high is the candle after 3 hours?

$20 - 7.5 = 12.5$ cm

After how many hours has this candle burnt down?

$20 : 2.5 = 8$

A tank with 300 ℓ loses 25 ℓ per minute. After how many minutes is it empty?

$300 : 25 = 12$

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Absolute and relative frequencies

A group threw the drawing pin 50 times. 31 times it landed on its back, 19 times on its side. Those are the absolute frequencies. As a proportion: $\tfrac{31}{50} = 0.62 = 62\%$ on its back. That is the relative frequency.

In a chance experiment you know the possible results, but you cannot predict which one will happen. Examples: coin, dice, spinner. A survey in the class also gives frequencies. If you assign each result its frequency, you get an assignment again.

To compare groups of different sizes, you need the relative frequency. It is a proportion and can be written as a fraction, a decimal or a percentage.

KEY POINT · FREQUENCIES

absolute frequency: how often a result occurs (a number)

relative frequency $= \dfrac{\text{absolute frequency}}{\text{number of all trials}}$, for example $\tfrac{31}{50} = 62\%$

All the relative frequencies together make $1 = 100\%$.

Language: “often” and “rarely” describe frequencies. The chance describes what you expect: with a dice, a six has a chance of 1 in 6.

Many trials: the more often you throw, the closer the relative frequency usually is to the chance. That is never certain for a single trial.

INTERACTIVE · COUNTING CHANCE

At the start 20 throws are already recorded. Throw 100 times and then 100 times more: how close do the bars come to the dashed line?

EXAMPLE 5 · A SURVEY

25 pupils were asked about their favourite subject. Maths 10, PE 8, art 4, German 3. Give the relative frequencies.

Subjectabsoluterelative
Maths10$\tfrac{10}{25} = 40\%$
PE8$\tfrac{8}{25} = 32\%$
Art4$\tfrac{4}{25} = 16\%$
German3$\tfrac{3}{25} = 12\%$

Check: $40 + 32 + 16 + 12 = 100\%$

EXAMPLE 6 · COMPARING

In class 6a 12 out of 30 read every day, in 6b 10 out of 20. In which class do people read more?

In absolute terms there are more in 6a. But relatively: 6a $\tfrac{12}{30} = 40\%$, 6b $\tfrac{10}{20} = 50\%$.

A larger proportion reads in 6b.

EXERCISES

A coin was thrown 40 times: 22 times heads. Give the absolute and the relative frequency of heads and of tails.

Heads: 22, $\tfrac{22}{40} = 0.55 = 55\%$. Tails: 18, $\tfrac{18}{40} = 0.45 = 45\%$.

A dice was thrown 60 times. The six came up 8 times. Is that more or less often than you would expect?

You would expect about $\tfrac16 \cdot 60 = 10$ times. 8 times is a little less often, but quite normal for 60 throws.

Do a survey in the class: how many brothers and sisters do you have? Show the absolute and relative frequencies in a table and a bar chart.

The solution depends on your class. Check: the relative frequencies must add up to $100\%$.

In basketball Lina scores 9 of 15 shots, Paul 13 of 20. Who is the more accurate shooter?

Lina: $\tfrac{9}{15} = 60\%$, Paul: $\tfrac{13}{20} = 65\%$. Paul scores relatively more often.

A spinner has a red section (half), a blue one (a third) and a green one (the rest). How large is the green section? How often do you expect each colour in 120 spins? Check with the spinner above.

Green: $1 - \tfrac12 - \tfrac13 = \tfrac16$. Expected: red about 60 times, blue about 40 times, green about 20 times. The real numbers differ from these.

TEST YOURSELF!

31 out of 50 throws: what is the relative frequency as a decimal?

$\tfrac{31}{50} = \tfrac{62}{100} = 0.62$

In 40 coin throws tails came up 18 times. What percentage is that?

$\tfrac{18}{40} = \tfrac{45}{100} = 45\%$

About how often do you expect a six in 60 throws?

$\tfrac16 \cdot 60 = 10$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Draw a coordinate system and plot the points $A(1, 2)$, $B(4, 2)$, $C(4, 5)$ and $D(1, 5)$. Join them. What do you get?

A square with side length 3.

Connecting with chapter 1.1: the relative frequency of heads is $0.48$ for 250 throws. How often did heads come up? Write $0.48$ as a fraction in its lowest terms.

$0.48 \cdot 250 = 120$ times. $0.48 = \tfrac{48}{100} = \tfrac{12}{25}$.

A taxi costs a basic fare of €3 and €2 per kilometre. Make a table for 0 to 5 km, draw a chart and set up an equation.

0 → €3, 1 → €5, 2 → €7, 3 → €9, 4 → €11, 5 → €13. $p = 3 + 2 \cdot s$. The points lie on a straight line that starts at 3.

Ana throws a dice 6 times and gets no six. She says: “Now the six has to come!” Is she right?

No. The dice has no memory. On the seventh throw too the chance of a six is 1 in 6. Only with very many throws do the frequencies usually even out.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

10,000 coin throws

In April 1940 the mathematician John Kerrich was visiting relatives in Copenhagen. Then German troops invaded Denmark, and Kerrich was held in a camp. To use the long time sensibly, he did an experiment: he threw a coin 10,000 times and wrote down every result.

In the end he had 5067 heads. That is a relative frequency of $\tfrac{5067}{10\,000} = 50.67\%$, very close to the chance of $50\%$. In the first throws the relative frequency still varied a lot. The more throws were added, the steadier it became.

Try it yourself: in the chance widget above, choose the coin and throw until you have 1000 throws. How far are you from $50\%$?

Source: John E. Kerrich, “An Experimental Introduction to the Theory of Probability”, Copenhagen 1946.
